items.summary: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were three young men from Judah taken to Babylon. They served in the Babylonian administration but refused King Nebuchadnezzar II's command to worship a golden image. They were thrown into a fiery furnace and miraculously survived.

Their Babylonian names were Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
They were companions of Daniel.
They refused to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image.

items.name: Belshazzar
items.subtitle: King at the Fall of Babylon
items.summary: Belshazzar was a Babylonian royal who ruled in Babylon as co-regent while his father Nabonidus was away. In Daniel 5, Belshazzar held a great feast and used sacred vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem. During the feast, mysterious writing appeared on the wall. Daniel interpreted the message as God's judgment on Belshazzar and his kingdom. That night Belshazzar was killed as Babylon fell.
quickFacts: Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus, the last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
He exercised royal authority in Babylon while Nabonidus was absent.
Daniel 5 records the famous writing on the wall during Belshazzar's feast.
Daniel interpreted the message as announcing the end of Belshazzar's kingdom.
Babylon fell to the Persian forces of Cyrus the Great in 539 BC.
items.certaintyNote: Belshazzar is independently known from Babylonian records. Ancient evidence identifies him as the son of King Nabonidus and shows that he exercised significant authority in Babylon, helping provide historical context for the account in Daniel 5.

items.name: Cyrus the Great
items.subtitle: Founder of the Persian Empire
items.summary: Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire and conquered Babylon in 539 BC. The Bible presents Cyrus as the ruler who allowed the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. His policies of restoring displaced peoples and local worship helped shape the early Persian period after the Babylonian Exile.
quickFacts: Cyrus founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire.
His forces captured Babylon in 539 BC.
The Bible credits Cyrus with permitting the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem.
Isaiah refers to Cyrus as God's anointed ruler for a specific purpose.
The Cyrus Cylinder is an important ancient artifact from his reign.
items.certaintyNote: Cyrus the Great is exceptionally well attested in ancient Persian, Babylonian, and Greek sources. His conquest of Babylon and policies toward subject peoples are independently documented outside the Bible.

items.name: The Fall of Babylon
items.subtitle: The Persian Conquest of Babylon
items.summary: In 539 BC, Babylon fell to the forces of Cyrus the Great, bringing the Neo-Babylonian Empire to an end and beginning Persian rule over the region. The event forms the historical setting for the end of Belshazzar's rule in Daniel 5 and helped set the stage for Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem under Persian authority.
quickFacts: Babylon fell to Persian forces in 539 BC.
Cyrus the Great became ruler of the Babylonian Empire's territories.
Daniel 5 places the death of Belshazzar on the night his kingdom fell.
Babylonian records also document the Persian capture of Babylon.
Persian rule later allowed Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem.
items.certaintyNote: The Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BC is firmly established by ancient historical records. Biblical and Babylonian sources describe the transition from Babylonian to Persian rule from different perspectives.

items.name: The Return from Exile
items.subtitle: Judah Returns from Babylonian Exile
items.summary: After Cyrus the Great conquered Babylon, Persian policy allowed groups of displaced peoples to return to their homelands. According to the biblical account, Cyrus authorized Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. This marked the beginning of a new period in Judah's history after decades of Babylonian exile.
quickFacts: The return began after Cyrus the Great conquered Babylon.
Cyrus authorized the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem.
Temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar were returned.
Zerubbabel became an important leader of the returning community.
The return from exile occurred in stages rather than as one single migration.
items.certaintyNote: The Persian conquest of Babylon and Cyrus's policies toward subject peoples are well established historically. The biblical books of Chronicles and Ezra provide the primary accounts of the Jewish return to Judah and the rebuilding of the temple.

items.name: The Cyrus Cylinder
items.subtitle: Ancient Record from the Reign of Cyrus
items.summary: The Cyrus Cylinder is an ancient clay cylinder inscribed in Babylonian cuneiform after Cyrus the Great conquered Babylon in 539 BC. The inscription describes Cyrus restoring temples and returning displaced religious images and peoples. Although it does not specifically mention the Jewish people or Jerusalem, it provides important historical context for the type of restoration policy described in the biblical book of Ezra.
quickFacts: The Cyrus Cylinder was discovered in Babylon in 1879.
It is written in Babylonian cuneiform on a clay cylinder.
The inscription was produced after Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC.
It describes Cyrus restoring temples and returning displaced peoples and religious objects.
The cylinder does not specifically mention Jerusalem or the Jewish exiles.
items.certaintyNote: The Cyrus Cylinder is a genuine ancient inscription from the reign of Cyrus the Great. It should not be treated as a copy of the biblical decree in Ezra, but it provides valuable historical evidence for Persian restoration policies consistent with the broader setting described in the Bible.

items.name: Zerubbabel
items.subtitle: Governor of Judah After the Exile
items.summary: Zerubbabel was a descendant of King David who became governor of Judah during the early Persian period. He led a group of Jewish exiles back to Jerusalem and played a major role in rebuilding the temple after the Babylonian Exile. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged Zerubbabel and the returned community during the rebuilding effort.
quickFacts: Zerubbabel was a descendant of King David.
He served as governor of Judah under Persian rule.
He helped lead Jewish exiles back to Jerusalem.
He played a central role in rebuilding the temple.
The prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged him during the rebuilding effort.
items.certaintyNote: Zerubbabel is described in several biblical books as a leader of the returned Jewish community during the Persian period. His role as governor fits the political structure of Judah under Persian imperial rule.

items.name: The Second Temple
items.subtitle: The Rebuilt Temple in Jerusalem
items.summary: The Second Temple was built in Jerusalem after the Jewish people returned from the Babylonian Exile. Construction began under the leadership of Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest but faced opposition and delays. Encouraged by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, the returned community resumed the work, and the temple was completed during the reign of the Persian king Darius I.
quickFacts: The Second Temple replaced Solomon's Temple, which had been destroyed by the Babylonians.
Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest were major leaders during the rebuilding.
The prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the people to complete the work.
The temple was completed around 516 BC during the reign of Darius I.
Centuries later, Herod the Great dramatically expanded and renovated the temple complex.
items.certaintyNote: The rebuilding of the temple belongs to the well-established Persian period of Judah's history. The biblical books of Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah provide the principal accounts of its reconstruction.

items.name: Haggai
items.subtitle: Prophet of the Temple Rebuilding
items.summary: Haggai was a prophet who ministered in Judah after the Babylonian Exile. He challenged the returned Jewish community to make rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem a priority. His messages encouraged Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest, and the people to resume construction of the Second Temple during the reign of the Persian king Darius I.
quickFacts: Haggai prophesied after the Jewish return from Babylonian Exile.
His recorded ministry took place during the reign of Darius I.
He urged the people to resume rebuilding the temple.
Haggai worked during the same period as the prophet Zechariah.
His messages specifically encouraged Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, and Joshua the high priest.
items.certaintyNote: The book of Haggai dates several of the prophet's messages precisely to the second year of Darius I, corresponding to 520 BC. This places Haggai within the well-established historical setting of Persian rule over Judah.

items.name: Zechariah
items.subtitle: Prophet of Restoration and Hope
items.summary: Zechariah was a prophet who ministered to the Jewish people after their return from Babylonian exile. Alongside Haggai, he encouraged the people to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem and called them to renewed faithfulness to God.
quickFacts: Zechariah began his prophetic ministry during the reign of Darius I.
He ministered during the same period as Haggai.
He encouraged the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem.
His book contains a series of symbolic visions.
Zechariah contains several passages associated with messianic hope.
items.certaintyNote: Zechariah's ministry is dated in the biblical text to the Persian period following the return from Babylonian exile.

items.name: Malachi
items.subtitle: Prophet of Covenant Faithfulness
items.summary: Malachi was a prophet who addressed the people of Judah after the return from Babylonian exile and the rebuilding of the Temple. He confronted careless worship, unfaithfulness, and spiritual complacency while calling the people back to covenant faithfulness.
quickFacts: Malachi ministered during the post-exilic period.
His message addressed problems with worship and the priesthood.
He called the people to renewed faithfulness to God's covenant.
Malachi spoke of a coming messenger who would prepare the way.
Malachi is the final book of the Old Testament in the Christian biblical order.
items.certaintyNote: The book of Malachi does not name a reigning king, so the precise date of the prophet's ministry is uncertain. It is generally placed during the Persian period after the rebuilding of the Temple.

sources.note: Primary biblical source for Malachi's prophetic message and ministry.

sources.title: Malachi 3:1–4
sources.note: Describes the coming messenger and the Lord's coming to his Temple.

sources.title: Malachi 4:4–6
sources.note: Concludes the book with a call to remember the law of Moses and a promise concerning Elijah.

items.name: Ezra
items.subtitle: Scribe and Teacher of the Law
items.summary: Ezra was a Jewish priest and scribe who traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem during the Persian period. He devoted himself to studying, practicing, and teaching the Law of God and played an important role in the spiritual renewal of the Jewish community after the Babylonian exile.
quickFacts: Ezra was both a priest and a skilled scribe.
He traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem during the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes.
Ezra devoted himself to studying, obeying, and teaching the Law of the Lord.
He led a group of Jewish exiles back to Jerusalem.
Ezra later appears with Nehemiah during a public reading and explanation of the Law.
items.certaintyNote: Ezra's ministry is placed during the Persian period. The traditional chronology places his arrival in Jerusalem during the reign of Artaxerxes I, though aspects of the chronology have been debated by scholars.

sources.title: Ezra 7–10
sources.note: Primary biblical account of Ezra's journey to Jerusalem and his ministry there.

sources.title: Nehemiah 8
sources.note: Describes Ezra publicly reading and explaining the Law to the assembled people.

items.name: Nehemiah
items.subtitle: Governor and Rebuilder of Jerusalem
items.summary: Nehemiah was a Jewish official in the Persian court who received permission from King Artaxerxes to return to Jerusalem. As governor of Judah, he led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, organized the city's defenses, and worked with Ezra to encourage spiritual and social reform among the people.
quickFacts: Nehemiah served as cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes.
He received permission to travel to Jerusalem and rebuild its walls.
The rebuilding effort faced opposition from surrounding leaders.
Jerusalem's wall was completed in fifty-two days according to the biblical account.
Nehemiah worked alongside Ezra during a period of religious and civic renewal.
items.certaintyNote: Nehemiah's governorship is placed during the reign of Artaxerxes I of Persia. The biblical account dates his journey to Jerusalem to the twentieth year of Artaxerxes.

sources.title: Nehemiah 1–7
sources.note: Primary biblical account of Nehemiah's journey to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the city's walls.

sources.title: Nehemiah 8
sources.note: Describes the public reading of the Law during the period of Ezra and Nehemiah.

sources.title: Nehemiah 13
sources.note: Records reforms carried out during Nehemiah's governorship.

items.name: Esther
items.subtitle: Jewish Queen of Persia
items.summary: Esther was a Jewish woman who became queen in the Persian Empire. When a plot threatened the destruction of the Jewish people, Esther risked her life by approaching the king and revealing both her identity and the danger facing her people. Her courage became central to the story behind the Jewish festival of Purim.
quickFacts: Esther was a Jewish woman living within the Persian Empire.
Her Hebrew name was Hadassah.
She was raised by her cousin Mordecai.
Esther became queen and used her position to intervene when the Jewish people were threatened.
The events recorded in Esther are associated with the origin of the festival of Purim.
items.certaintyNote: The book of Esther places its events in the Persian royal court at Susa. The king called Ahasuerus in the biblical text is traditionally identified with Xerxes I, who reigned from 486 to 465 BC.

sources.title: Esther 1–10
sources.note: Primary biblical account of Esther, Mordecai, the Persian court, and the deliverance of the Jewish people.

sources.title: Esther 4:13–16
sources.note: Records Mordecai's appeal to Esther and her decision to approach the king despite the personal risk.

sources.title: Esther 9:20–28
sources.note: Connects the events of Esther with the establishment of the festival of Purim.

items.name: Mordecai
items.subtitle: Jewish Leader in the Persian Court
items.summary: Mordecai was a Jewish man living in Susa during the Persian period and the cousin and guardian of Esther. He uncovered a plot against the king and later refused to bow before Haman. When Haman sought the destruction of the Jewish people, Mordecai urged Esther to use her position as queen to intervene.
quickFacts: Mordecai was Esther's cousin and became her guardian after the death of her parents.
He lived in Susa, one of the major royal cities of the Persian Empire.
Mordecai uncovered a plot to assassinate the Persian king.
His refusal to bow before Haman helped set the central conflict of the book of Esther in motion.
Mordecai eventually rose to a position of great authority within the Persian government.
items.certaintyNote: Mordecai is known primarily from the biblical book of Esther. The narrative places him in the Persian royal city of Susa during the reign of Ahasuerus, traditionally identified with Xerxes I.

sources.title: Esther 2–10
sources.note: Primary biblical account of Mordecai's role in the Persian court and the deliverance of the Jewish people.

sources.title: Esther 4:13–17
sources.note: Records Mordecai's appeal urging Esther to intervene on behalf of her people.

sources.title: Esther 10:1–3
sources.note: Describes Mordecai's high position and influence within the Persian kingdom.

items.name: Haman
items.subtitle: Enemy of the Jews in the Persian Court
items.summary: Haman was a high-ranking official in the Persian court during the reign of Ahasuerus. After Mordecai refused to bow before him, Haman became enraged and devised a plan to destroy the Jewish people throughout the empire. His plot was ultimately exposed by Queen Esther, leading to his downfall.
quickFacts: Haman was promoted to a high position by King Ahasuerus.
He became furious when Mordecai refused to bow before him.
Haman cast lots, called pur, to determine a date for his plan against the Jewish people.
Esther exposed Haman's plot during a banquet with the king.
Haman was executed on the structure he had prepared for Mordecai.
items.certaintyNote: Haman is known from the biblical book of Esther, which places him in the Persian royal court during the reign of Ahasuerus, traditionally identified with Xerxes I.

sources.title: Esther 3–8
sources.note: Primary biblical account of Haman's rise, his plot against the Jewish people, and his downfall.

sources.title: Esther 3:7–15
sources.note: Describes Haman's use of the pur and the royal decree against the Jewish people.

sources.title: Esther 7:1–10
sources.note: Records Esther exposing Haman's plot and Haman's subsequent execution.

items.name: Xerxes I (Ahasuerus)
items.subtitle: Persian King in the Story of Esther
items.summary: Xerxes I was a king of the Persian Empire and is traditionally identified with Ahasuerus, the ruler described in the book of Esther. The biblical account places Esther, Mordecai, and Haman within his royal court at Susa, where a threat against the Jewish people developed into a dramatic struggle for survival.
quickFacts: Xerxes I ruled the Persian Empire from 486 to 465 BC.
He was the son and successor of Darius I.
The Ahasuerus of Esther is traditionally identified with Xerxes I.
Susa was one of the major royal centers of the Persian Empire.
Xerxes also led a major Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BC.
items.certaintyNote: The identification of the biblical Ahasuerus with Xerxes I is widely accepted, although the book of Esther uses the Hebrew royal name Ahasuerus rather than the Greek form Xerxes.

sources.title: Esther 1–10
sources.note: Primary biblical account of Ahasuerus and the events involving Esther, Mordecai, and Haman.

sources.title: Esther 1:1–9
sources.note: Introduces Ahasuerus as ruler of a vast Persian realm and describes the royal court at Susa.

sources.title: Esther 7–8
sources.note: Describes the king's response to Esther's revelation of Haman's plot.

items.name: Job
items.subtitle: Righteous Sufferer of the Land of Uz
items.summary: Job is the central figure of the biblical book that bears his name. Described as a righteous and prosperous man living in the land of Uz, Job experiences the loss of his wealth, children, and health. His story explores suffering, faithfulness, human wisdom, and the limits of human understanding before God.
quickFacts: Job is described as blameless, upright, and one who feared God.
He lived in a place called the land of Uz.
Job's friends Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar came to mourn and speak with him.
Much of the book consists of poetic discussions about suffering, justice, and wisdom.
Job is also named in Ezekiel as an example of righteousness.
items.location: Land of Uz / Ancient Near East
items.certaintyNote: The historical period and precise location of Job are uncertain. The book places Job outside Israel in the land of Uz, while scholars continue to debate when the book reached its literary form.

sources.title: Job 1–42
sources.note: Primary biblical account of Job, his suffering, his discussions with his friends, God's response, and Job's restoration.

sources.title: Ezekiel 14:14, 20
sources.note: Names Job alongside Noah and Daniel as examples of righteousness.

sources.title: The Historical Context of the Book of Job — Yale University Press
sources.note: Academic discussion of the language, historical context, and ancient Near Eastern background of the Book of Job.

items.name: Abraham
items.subtitle: Patriarch of the Covenant
items.summary: Abraham is a central patriarch in the biblical story and the father of Isaac. According to Genesis, God called him to leave his homeland and travel to Canaan, promising to make him into a great nation and to bless the nations through him. Abraham's life became foundational to the biblical story of Israel, covenant, faith, and promise.
quickFacts: Abraham was originally called Abram.
Genesis describes his journey from Mesopotamia toward the land of Canaan.
God's covenant with Abraham included promises concerning descendants and land.
Abraham and Sarah became the parents of Isaac.
Abraham is an important figure in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
items.certaintyNote: Abraham is known primarily through biblical tradition. There is no currently accepted direct archaeological evidence identifying Abraham as an individual, and the precise historical setting of the patriarchal narratives remains debated among scholars.

sources.title: Genesis 11–25
sources.note: Primary biblical account of Abraham's life, journeys, family, and covenant.

sources.title: Remembering Abraham: Culture, Memory, and History in the Hebrew Bible — Oxford Academic
sources.note: Scholarly study of Abraham, biblical memory, and the historical traditions contained in the patriarchal narratives.

items.name: Isaac
items.subtitle: Son of Promise
items.summary: Isaac was the son of Abraham and Sarah and an important patriarch in the biblical story. His birth fulfilled God's promise that Abraham and Sarah would have a son. Isaac later became the father of Esau and Jacob, continuing the covenant family through which the biblical story of Israel developed.
quickFacts: Isaac was the son of Abraham and Sarah.
His birth was presented as the fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham.
Abraham was tested when God commanded him to offer Isaac.
Isaac married Rebekah.
Isaac and Rebekah became the parents of the twins Esau and Jacob.
items.certaintyNote: Isaac is known primarily through the biblical patriarchal narratives. There is no currently accepted direct archaeological evidence identifying Isaac as an individual, and the precise historical setting of the patriarchs remains debated.

sources.title: Genesis 17–35
sources.note: Primary biblical material concerning Isaac, his family, and his place in the patriarchal narratives.

sources.title: Remembering Abraham: Culture, Memory, and History in the Hebrew Bible — Oxford Academic
sources.note: Scholarly examination of the patriarchal traditions, historical memory, and the biblical world in which the stories of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are preserved.

items.name: Jacob (Israel)
items.subtitle: Patriarch and Father of the Twelve Tribes
items.summary: Jacob was the son of Isaac and Rebekah and the grandson of Abraham. According to Genesis, he received the name Israel after wrestling with a mysterious divine figure. Jacob became the father of twelve sons whose descendants were associated with the twelve tribes of Israel, making him a foundational figure in the biblical story of the nation.
quickFacts: Jacob was the younger twin brother of Esau.
His parents were Isaac and Rebekah.
Genesis describes Jacob receiving the name Israel.
Jacob had twelve sons who became associated with the tribes of Israel.
Jacob's son Joseph rose to power in Egypt, where Jacob's family eventually settled.
items.certaintyNote: Jacob is known primarily through biblical tradition. There is no currently accepted direct archaeological evidence identifying Jacob as an individual, and scholars distinguish between the historical origins of Israel and the later literary form of the Jacob narratives.

sources.title: Genesis 25–50
sources.note: Primary biblical account of Jacob, his family, his name Israel, and the development of the twelve sons of Jacob.

sources.title: Remembering Jacob in the Late Persian/Early Hellenistic Era — Oxford Academic
sources.note: Scholarly study examining Jacob as a figure representing Israel and the development and remembrance of Jacob traditions.
